Likewise, the RACK1-40S interface is well described and mutations can easily be made to disrupt this. The mutant should be used in key experiments including 6b, 6f, 7c.
Response: We have added experiments showing that recruitment of mRNAs encoding autophagy proteins to phagophores in RACK1 knockdown cells is rescued by wild-type RACK1, but not RACK1 Thr50 or RACK1 R36D/K38E which is required for its binding to ribosomes (Fig.6q, r). This shows, for the first time, that RACK1 binding to complexes involved in phagophore formation and its binding to ribosomes are required to recruit mRNAs to the phagophore site.
b) RACK is already known to positively regulate autophagy (PMIDs: 22562043, 26549445) and therefore Fig 7d and 7e do not provide any new information. The reduction in puncta upon transient knockdown (7e) is therefore expected and it is unclear how this could reflect a localized translation effect.
Response: As we said above, it is extremely difficult to show a functional impact of local translation in the field in general, because of challenges like these of separating RACK1’s local effects on translation, from its effects on translation elsewhere in the cell or autophagosome formation. We have rewritten key parts of the paper to temper statements that our findings demonstrate that local translation is required for sustained autophagy. Our data in Fig.6s shows that formation of autophagosomes is disrupted by mutations in RACK1 which block its association with ribosomes. This data provides improved support for the hypothesis that local translation is important for autophagy.
c) And why do the RACK1 experiments generally only address a subset of transcripts from those in Figure 3? Is this because RACK1 is only regulating translation of some of these?
Why are the transcripts in 7c not the same as the proteins in 7d? These figures should support each other. Why also, are the authors only showing 3 transcripts in 7c + MTCO2 as a control, what about all the others from 6b?
Response: Experiments in Fig.7c (now is Fig 6c) require proximity labeling pulldown from ribosome density gradient fractions. The yields are not high, and we only recovered enough RNA to do RT-qPCR for 4 mRNAs involved in autophagy (ATG3, ATG12, VPS34, DFCP1) and a negative control (MTCO2) (Fig.6c). This demonstrates the phenomena is not restricted to a single mRNA. We do not have antibodies that work well for some of the proteins, so we did not test the protein for every mRNA evaluated. We used antibodies for some multiple key proteins in autophagy (ATG3, LC3, ATG5-12). We also validated more autophagy related proteins in the new Fig. 6d-k.
d) If only some mRNAs are selectively translated near the phagophore in a RACK1-dependent manner, what would be the mechanism by which this occurs? The authors should investigate whether there are certain features pertaining to the translated mRNAs including sequence motifs or other means of post-transcriptional regulation, to at least touch upon this mechanism.
Response: We agree it would be great to identify an RNA sequence or structure motif that enables recruitment of these mRNAs to phagophores. This would require several additional figures of experiments to identify and characterize. For example, Fazal first identified local translation in proximity to mitochondria (Cell 2019), and subsequently began to identify RNA features required for this (Qin Nat. Comm 2021). We feel this is more appropriate for a follow-up manuscript. We have nonetheless added data showing that the mRNA localization observed requires binding of ribosomes to RACK1 (Fig.6q, r) and the mRNA (puromycin, Fig.5a, Supplementary Fig.2f).
Additional comments
4) It is unclear if there are any endogenous Ab stains throughout the manuscript. For instance, the authors mention that they are looking at endogenous RACK1 in Figure 6c. However, the figure shows RACK1-GFP? Also, the authors mention that they are showing endogenous DFCP1 and LC3B signals in Fig 1c. But in these cells, they are expressing the APEX2-tagged constructs. So how can it be said that the puncta co-localize with endogenous proteins? It is understandable that not everything can be done with endogenous stains, but at least some key data should be confirmed with endogenous stains and the authors should be more careful in their experimental descriptions.
Response: We have used antibodies for endogenous proteins in three places. In Fig.1a we show the proximity-labeling with APEX2-DFCP1 and APEX2-LC3 occurs in discrete spots as expected and these co-localize with DFCP1 and LC3B detected with antibodies. In Supp. 1d we also show that endogenous p62 which is recruited to phagophores (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-20185-1) also co-localizes with proximity-labeling from APEX2-DFCP1. Proximity-ligation assays in Fig.5e use antibodies recognizing endogenous RACK1 and DFCP1 to show that these endogenous proteins are in proximity to one another.
5) Figures 1a, b, c do not present any novel information. They show well-known effects of drugs on LC3BII and polysome profiles. This type of data should – at most – be presented in the supplementary data.
Response: We have moved Fig.1a and Fig.1b to the supplementary data. For Fig.1c (now is Fig .1a), we keep it in the main figure to confirm the specificity of this proximity-based biotinylation.
6) In general, the methods, legends and experimental details are poorly described and often lacking details regarding eg. timing and concentrations of treatments. Also, the handling of qRT-PCR data and methods of normalization are inadequately described and seem variable, sometimes displaying Ct values, sometimes displaying data “vs. omit” and sometimes “vs. omit and input”.
Response: We have revisited methods and figure legends to ensure critical details are included. We consistently normalize proximity-labeling experiments to the omit (without H O ). The 2 2
exceptions to this are when we assess effects on translation in proximity to phagophores after RACK1 or NUFIP1 depletion, where the global translation in input is also likely affected.
7) While it is OK to perform qRTpcrs on the pooled sub, light and heavy polysome fractions, the quality of the full polysome profiles should be verified by protein extractions from individual non-pooled fractions in order to verify the presence of 40S, 60S, monosomes, polysomes in the expected fractions. It would additionally be useful to see the full profile for some of the mRNAs to understand how enrichment in some fractions may affect other fractions.
Response: We have included A260 profiles of the ribosome fractionation as standard in the field to show the expected peaks. We also showed the expected effect of mTOR inhibition and EDTA on the A260 profiles as the most common way to validate that peaks are due to ribosomes identity (Fig.3f and Supplementary Fig.1b). We have now also added blots of small and large ribosome proteins which fractionate as expected (Supplementary Fig.2c).
8) For Figures 3b and c, why are these two graphs separated and why are different controls used in the two graphs? Fig 3c EGFR in fact looks to be 6-7 fold upregulated between “input H” vs. “pulldown H”. Wouldn’t this indicate a similar enrichment as seen for all autophagy transcripts in 3b?
Response: These are always relative measures. There was a higher background level in this experiment and so more EGFR mRNA was identified. As EGFR mRNA will localize to ER not very far from the phagophore formation site this is not entirely unexpected if labeling of the DFCP1-APEX2 system was a bit too strong here. The important point is that p62 mRNA is much more highly enriched in proximity to phagophores vs. EGFR mRNA in this experiment. Because of the inconsistency in this data, we have removed it from the paper. Data with other negative and positive controls remains in all other figures.
9) Figure 1d shows enrichment of 18S in the pulldown. Is this also the case for 28S and 5.8S? In later figures there are discrepancies between small and large subunit rRNAs. Surely the full ribosome would be required to be present for this translation task. The authors should test this more extensively and comment.
Response: Fig.1d (now is Fig.1b, c) shows 18S and Fig.5a shows 18S and 28S. We also show that heavy polysomes containing multiple autophagy mRNAs are located in proximity to DFCP1 (Fig.3f, g), translation occurs there (Fig.3a-e), and nascent proteins involved in autophagy are present there (Fig.3h, i). Together this shows with multiple independent approaches that active ribosomes are present in proximity to DFCP1.
Minor comments:
It would have been helpful with line nrs and page nrs.
Western blots should include MW markers
The authors should be careful to distinguish between MTOR and MTORC1
There are several mistakes with the references to wrong papers. See eg. #44 and others.
Response: We have made these changes.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have addressed many of my concerns. Still, I have remaining critical points that must be addressed, including the need for additional evidence, in order for the work to support the conclusions and claims of the authors. In addition, there are methodology descriptions and statistical analysis that are lacking at several places. Some initial questions also still remain unanswered.
Regarding original point 1a)
I do not find any methodological description of the APEX2-seq, only the heatmap which contains minimal information. Are these changes significant? How many replicates is this based on? Such standard information on the setup, inclusion of p-values etc. must be added as a minimum to support any claims.
There are several inconsistencies between 1b and 1f which substantiate the previous concern about the robustness of the data. For instance, p62, a key target in 1b and throughout the entire paper, seems even downregulated in proximity to DFCP1 in the sequencing? How do the authors reconcile such contradictory data?
Although it is understandable that data was collected over years, with slightly changing focus on transcripts over time, this is an issue encountered by most researchers when publishing. Considering the additional concerns introduced from the sequencing, together with the previous inconsistencies that are still there, Figure 1 as a whole comes across as confusing and still requires consolidation by performing some repeats for each panel, to show consistency for a selected group of transcripts and controls.
Regarding original point 1b)
Fig 1e is now added as an essential control to Fig 1b and the authors state “The mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy which were enriched in proximity to DFCP1, were not enriched in proximity to a diffuse cytoplasmic protein (Cytoplasmic V5-tag) or Perilipin (Fig.1e). Similarly, these mRNAs were not enriched in proximity to NPM1 (Fig.1e).” If Fig 1e should function as a proper negative control (for those transcripts enriched at DFCP1, as stated) it should certainly be done on the same set of transcripts, not on new ones or omitting old ones. Considering the importance of this control, this data is key and must be provided. Fig 1e should also be depicted in the same way as 1b/c, with statistical significance calculated relative to inputs, to allow for comparison.
Regarding original point 1c)
It seems that the FIP200 -/- cells were generated in this study (as stated in author contributions section). If this is the case, a description of their generation and validation is lacking. If they are previoulsy described, the authors should provide a reference. Also, the western in Fig 2g should include blotting for FIP200. In Fig 2h the results from the FIP200-/- cells should be depicted in comparison to WT (as in 2g), including a statistical comparison between the two cell types. A KO cell line cannot stand alone as a negative result without comparison to its WT counterpart from the same experiment. This is standard practice.
Regarding original point 2a)
Even if phagophores emerge from ribosome free regions of the ER, there are likely at any given moment, multiple ribosomes in proximity to a phagophore, especially in conditions of ribophagy induction by mTOR inhibition. The authors should comment this in the manuscript. This relates to the concern below about excluding an impact of ribophagy.
Regarding original points 2c&e)
The previous comment: “To enhance the credibility of their claim, the authors should try to understand how ribosomes performing localized translation could be positioned to avoid their random engulfment” was not replied to. Ribosomes are not comparable in abundance, size or nature to the proteins mentioned by the authors that avoid degradation.
The role of NUFIP1 in ribophagy has been thoroughly refuted (PMID: 32612236) and it is widely acknowledged in the field that the original findings from (PMID: 29700228) are not reproducible. Therefore, the NUFIP knockdown experiments do not provide value to the manuscript and should be removed. This still leaves the general concern that the findings may be due to a bystander effect of ribophagy, which should be adressed by different means.
Regarding original point 3b)
The authors rightly state that a functional impact of localized translation is debatable, also leaving the biological consequences of their own work questionable. Even more so when potential interference from ribophagy is not excluded (as described above). The authors state that they have rewritten key parts of the paper to “temper statements that our findings demonstrate that local translation is required for sustained autophagy”. Yet there is still even speculation on this in the abstract and elsewhere. Please temper further and point out all changes by indicating line number.
Regarding original point 3c)
The lack of consistency is still problematic between 6c and 6d because without this consistency, the idea that localized translation of specific mRNA leads to local protein production is simply not supported. The corresponding antibodies for the four transcripts in 6c are widely used, available and suitable for western blotting (as shown extensively in the litterature). This includes DFCP1 that the authors even use themselves (Supp. Fig 1F). The experiments should be done to fullfil this.
Regarding original point 4)
The previous question is not answered: “the authors mention that they are showing endogenous DFCP1 and LC3B signals in Fig 1c. But in these cells, they are expressing the APEX2-tagged constructs. So how can it be said that the puncta co-localize with endogenous proteins?” Again, please answer: How can the authors claim that the signals come from the endogenous proteins? The Abs surely recognize the APEX-tagged proteins, which the authors even show are present at several fold higher amounts?
Regarding original point 6)
The authors explain why APEX-qpcr data is sometimes displayed relative to input or not. 1e should be displayed relative to input, according to this explanation. With statistics, as mentioned above.
Regarding original point 9)
The previous question is not answered: “Figure 1d shows enrichment of 18S in the pulldown. Is this also the case for 28S and 5.8S? Please answer. The other findings mentioned here only indirectly adress this point.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have done an excellent job in addressing the main concerns that were outlined previously and have adequately responded to the criticisms. Below are a few minor points that could be addressed in a revised version to improve the paper.
-In Figure 1F, the authors describe conducting RNA-seq of mRNAs purified from their proximity labeling reactions for APEX-tagged DFCP1, CytoV5 and Perilipin. However, they provided very little information about this experiment. It would seem strategically advantageous to give more information about these results, e.g. how many RNAs were identified in each purification, whether these had any functional signatures via GO-term enrichment analyses, etc. This data would enhance the paper without much additional work and could be added as a supplement, with some elements included in the main figure. -Similar to the comment above, in Figure 3h-I the authors present results of MS profiling datasets. It would again be to their benefit to give more information about these results (e.g. number of proteins identified in the different labeling assays, functional signatures, etc).
-Line 67: ‘… autophagosomes are formed in a cell.’
-Line 76: ‘Once activated, the ULK1 complex…’
-Line 247: ‘… translation of several proteins involved in autophagy is required to…’

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: We have added the requested details on the APEX2seq sample preparation and RNAseq analysis to the Methods section.
Are these changes significant? How many replicates is this based on? Such standard information on the setup, inclusion of p-values etc. must be added as a minimum to support any claims.
Response: The p-value of each RNA in the APEX2-seq datasets was determined by comparing the three replicates of H O labeling versus H O omission using an independent T-test (see Fig.1f of the Source data file). This confirms that many of the mRNA enrichments in proximity to DFCP1 are not random.
There are several inconsistencies between 1b and 1f which substantiate the previous concern about the robustness of the data. For instance, p62, a key target in 1b and throughout the entire paper, seems even downregulated in proximity to DFCP1 in the sequencing? How do the authors reconcile such contradictory data?
Response: We included >80 mRNAs from a comprehensive list of proteins involved in autophagy from a recent review from the Mizushima group (PMID: 36635405) in Fig.1f. When such a large number of mRNAs are tested, statistically, with a p=0.05 cutoff we will have several mRNAs that do not show their actual effects. Therefore, statistically, some inconsistencies must be expected. The overarching message of the APEX2-seq analysis is that a very large number of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy are enriched in proximity to DFCP1 compared to the three control APEX2 fusion proteins.
This is shown with multiple independent methods (FISH, RT-qPCR, RNAseq). Each method has inherent biases in the RNAs it will detect, and measure based on RNA structure, interactions, and RNA modifications. For example, FISH probes may be impacted by RNA structure or a RNA’s accessibility. Sequencing and RT-qPCR methods can be biased by changes in RNA purification or an enzyme’s ability to reverse-transcribe or ligate an RNA that is chemically modified (e.g biotinylated) or highly structured. This is well-established with the contrast between standard RNAseq and TGIRT RNAseq. In our experiments, the biotinylated RNAs pulled down for RNA-seq were isolated from streptavidin beads using TRIzol, whereas the RNA for RT-qPCR was directly reverse-transcribed while bound to the beads, different reverse-transcriptases and ligation steps were involved. Such minor variations/inconsistencies are to be expected when one notes the complexity and inherent biases of each method. Collectively, the data with many mRNAs and independent methods reinforces the conclusion that many mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy are enriched in proximity to phagophores.
Although it is understandable that data was collected over years, with slightly changing focus on transcripts over time, this is an issue encountered by most researchers when publishing. Considering the additional concerns introduced from the sequencing, together with the previous inconsistencies that are still there, Figure 1 as a whole comes across as confusing and still requires consolidation by performing some repeats for each panel, to show consistency for a selected group of transcripts and controls.
Response: Each panel of Figure 1 already includes data from a minimum of three repeats of the same experiment. Throughout the paper, we have shown the enrichment of these mRNAs in a minimum of three biological replicates in Fig.1, Fig. 5a, Fig. 5f, and Fig 6r confirming that these results are highly reproducible over 12 or more replicates of the experiment.
Regarding original point 1b)
Fig 1e is now added as an essential control to Fig 1b and the authors state “The mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy which were enriched in proximity to DFCP1, were not enriched in proximity to a diffuse cytoplasmic protein (Cytoplasmic V5-tag) or Perilipin (Fig.1e). Similarly, these mRNAs were not enriched in proximity to NPM1 (Fig.1e).” If Fig 1e should function as a proper negative control (for those transcripts enriched at DFCP1, as stated) it should certainly be done on the same set of transcripts, not on new ones or omitting old ones. Considering the importance of this control, this data is key and must be provided. Fig 1e should also be depicted in the same way as 1b/c, with statistical significance calculated relative to inputs, to allow for comparison.
Response: We encourage the reviewer to consider all data provided. Three of the six mRNAs included in Fig.1b were tested on the negative controls to confirm a pattern. One must also consider that APEX2-seq data displayed in Fig.1 further shows across over 80 mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy that most are enriched in proximity to DFCP1 compared to all three control APEX2 fusions. These should compensate for minor changes in which mRNAs were tested in Fig.1b and e.
We tested effects on inputs in H₂O₂ treated and untreated groups repeatedly throughout the paper (Fig.1b, c, Fig.2e, f, h, Fig.3g, Fig.5a, f). As the only difference between these two samples is a 1 min H₂O₂ treatment, it is not surprising that consistently there was no change between these input samples. Therefore, the result would be identical in Fig.1e whether this was included or not. We considered it superfluous and unnecessary to analyze input samples in Fig.1e for this reason. The key control (H₂O₂ omit pulldown) is used for normalization instead.
Regarding original point 1c)
It seems that the FIP200 -/- cells were generated in this study (as stated in author contributions section). If this is the case, a description of their generation and validation is lacking. If they are previously described, the authors should provide a reference. Also, the western in Fig 2g should include blotting for FIP200. In Fig 2h the results from the FIP200-/- cells should be depicted in comparison to WT (as in 2g), including a statistical comparison between the two cell types. A KO cell line cannot stand alone as a negative result without comparison to its WT counterpart from the same experiment. This is standard practice.
Response: A description of the generation of this cell line using CRISPR has been added to the methods. The FIP200 knockouts were validated by Sanger sequencing (shown below). Both alleles of FIP200 showed frameshifting mutations. Neither we, nor our collaborator (Ryan Russell) could manage to detect FIP200 by Western blot. We therefore showed that these FIP200 knockout cells exhibit the established phenotype: lack of induction of LC3-II, and accumulation of p62 in response to mTOR. While we understand the reviewer’s perspective about including the wild-type control, we believe that the fact that mRNA enrichment in proximity to DFCP1 was reproducible in 12 replicates across Fig.1, Fig. 5a, Fig. 5f, and Fig 6r makes the same point.
Regarding original point 2a)
Even if phagophores emerge from ribosome free regions of the ER, there are likely at any given moment, multiple ribosomes in proximity to a phagophore, especially in conditions of ribophagy induction by mTOR inhibition. The authors should comment this in the manuscript. This relates to the concern below about excluding an impact of ribophagy.
Response: We do not exclude that ribosomes could localize to phagophores for degradation. We have expanded our analysis of the potential impact of ribophagy in the Discussion now.
Available literature on ribophagy, that the reviewer tells us is the most reliable below, states that ribophagy is a non-selective bystander process of autophagy. Therefore, ribophagy would NOT cause selective enrichment of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy as our evidence demonstrates using RT-qPCR, RNAseq and FISH.
The reviewer’s preferred reference on ribophagy from Heeseon et al. in Wade Harper’s lab (PMID: 32612236) finds only a 3-4% almost undetectable decrease in ribosomes and this only after 24 h of mTOR inhibition. Data from other publications on ribophagy (Lopez et al. Cell Reports 2023, Wyant et al. Science 2018) show that ribophagy is undetectable until at least 10-24 h of mTOR inhibition or 72 h of senescence induction. No published evidence shows any detectable ribophagy at the time points used in the experiments in our article of 2-4 h mTOR inhibition.
Finally, no data suggests that ribosomes degraded by autophagy are actively translating. Indeed, current models suggest these ribosomes are defective. Our data demonstrates that mRNAs encoding autophagy proteins are in heavy polysomes in proximity to phagophores. Our pulse-chase labeling also shows selective accumulation of nascent ATG3, ATG5, p62, DFCP1 and VPS34 proteins in proximity to phagophores. These findings again contradict current models of ribophagy.
In sum, our data contradicts a role for ribophagy in three key areas: (i) selectivity for specific mRNAs, (ii) translation of these mRNAs (heavy polysomes, SILAC) and (iii) a time frame incompatible with detectable ribophagy. Nonetheless, we have modified the Discussion substantially to more fully analyze these issues and raise the possibility that ribophagy could account for the presence of some ribosomes at phagophores.
Regarding original points 2c&e)
The previous comment: “To enhance the credibility of their claim, the authors should try to understand how ribosomes performing localized translation could be positioned to avoid their random engulfment” was not replied to. Ribosomes are not comparable in abundance, size or nature to the proteins mentioned by the authors that avoid degradation.
Response: There could be simple explanations. For example, phagophores form a cup-shaped structure which expand and engulf substrates in a specific direction, positioning ribosomes on the exterior surface of the phagophore or underneath this cup would allow them to escape degradation while producing relevant proteins in proximity to forming autophagosomes. We do not exclude that ribosomes translating mRNAs encoding autophagy proteins could be degraded at some point by autophagy, after translating autophagy proteins. If ribophagy is undetectable (Heeseon et al.) at the time frames of mTOR inhibition we use, it is not possible to study it and exclude it.
The role of NUFIP1 in ribophagy has been thoroughly refuted (PMID: 32612236) and it is widely acknowledged in the field that the original findings from (PMID: 29700228) are not reproducible. Therefore, the NUFIP knockdown experiments do not provide value to the manuscript and should be removed. This still leaves the general concern that the findings may be due to a bystander effect of ribophagy, which should be addressed by different means.
Response: While the reviewer is evidently an expert on ribophagy, and is privileged to knowledge from private discussions, the published peer-reviewed literature is not as definitive. For the time being, we have retained this data in the paper and whenever we mention NUFIP1 we state that its role in ribophagy is disputed. If the editor agrees with the reviewer, we can remove data on NUFIP1.
As we outlined above in response to original point 2a there are multiple reasons why ribophagy cannot account for our results. (i) Ribophagy as non-selective would not cause selective enrichment of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy, (ii) ribosomes targeted for ribophagy are poly-ubiquitinated and are believed to be defective and not translating, while our data shows these mRNAs are in heavy polysomes and producing nascent protein in proximity to phagophores, and finally (iii) ribophagy is undetectable in the time frames we study.
How can we perform an experiment to test the impact of ribophagy in a time frame when ribophagy is undetectable? Furthermore, even if ribophagy did meaningfully occur at 2-4 h after mTOR inhibition, if it is non-selective there is no way to specifically interfere with ribophagy without affecting phagophore/autophagosome formation, which is required for the selective recruitment of the mRNAs in our system. This makes it impossible to test the impact of ribophagy.
Regarding original point 3b)
The authors rightly state that a functional impact of localized translation is debatable, also leaving the biological consequences of their own work questionable. Even more so when potential interference from ribophagy is not excluded (as described above). The authors state that they have rewritten key parts of the paper to “temper statements that our findings demonstrate that local translation is required for sustained autophagy”. Yet there is still even speculation on this in the abstract and elsewhere. Please temper further and point out all changes by indicating line number.
Response: We have made additional changes in the abstract (line 33 and 35). We have been careful not to firmly conclude that local translation promotes autophagy and revisited the text again to ensure this. Our statements suggest this possibility based on evidence from multiple independent methods that these mRNAs are both selectively enriched and translated there (polysomes, nascent translation proteomics). In this context, it would seem highly unusual to not suggest that local translation could help promote autophagy, while insisting that ribophagy which (i) does not detectably occur in this time frame after mTOR inhibition, (ii) is not selective like our data, and (iii) likely targets disabled ribosomes explains our data. Objectively weighing the literature and our evidence it seems extremely unlikely that ribophagy substantially accounts for our results. We also note that three other expert reviewers are comfortable with our conclusions in the current format.
Regarding original point 3c)
The lack of consistency is still problematic between 6c and 6d because without this consistency, the idea that localized translation of specific mRNA leads to local protein production is simply not supported. The corresponding antibodies for the four transcripts in 6c are widely used, available and suitable for western blotting (as shown extensively in the litterature). This includes DFCP1 that the authors even use themselves (Supp. Fig 1F). The experiments should be done to fullfil this.
Response: We have added data showing that RACK1 knockdown also reduces levels of VPS34. More Western blots for more proteins are always possible, but we have already shown the effects on 5 proteins (ATG5-12, LC3, p62 and NBR1, VPS34), including 2 of 4 from Fig.6c (heavy polysome profiling with RACK1 depletion). We believe this adequately demonstrates an impact on translation of proteins involved in autophagy, and the other 3 reviewers concur.
Regarding original point 4)
The previous question is not answered: “the authors mention that they are showing endogenous DFCP1 and LC3B signals in Fig 1c. But in these cells, they are expressing the APEX2-tagged constructs. So how can it be said that the puncta co-localize with endogenous proteins?” Again, please answer: How can the authors claim that the signals come from the endogenous proteins? The Abs surely recognize the APEX-tagged proteins, which the authors even show are present at several fold higher amounts?
Response: We encourage the reviewer to consider the full array of data we provide. APEX2 cell lines were generated and validated by our collaborator Dr. Christian Behrends, an expert in APEX2 labeling cell lines. APEX2-DFCP1 biotinylation signal co-localizes tightly with mCherry-DFCP1, with an antibody vs. DFCP1 (Fig.1) and with endogenous p62 (Supplementary Fig.1), which is recruited to the phagophore during its initiation (e.g. PMID:33397898). We have added data confirming the colocalization of APEX2-myc-DFCP1 baits to biotin-positive puncta (labelled with streptavidin) in revised Supplementary Fig.1e. Biotinylated foci are small in agreement with precise localized labeling. In addition, ATG14 proteins were successfully precipitated by streptavidin beads after biotinylation in their generated APEX2-DFCP1 cell lines (revised Supplementary Fig.1f). This construct also biotinylates and selectively enriches a broad collection of proteins involved in autophagosome formation including ATG3, ATG12, ATG5, ATG16L1 and VPS34 (Fig.3h, i), again demonstrating that it localizes appropriately to forming autophagosomes.
Collectively, this provides a wide array of data from independent methods that show that the DFCP1 proximity labeling system is appropriately and precisely localized.
Regarding original point 6)
The authors explain why APEX-qpcr data is sometimes displayed relative to input or not. 1e should be displayed relative to input, according to this explanation. With statistics, as mentioned above.
Response: The reviewer may have misunderstood what we tried to say. Normalizing to input RNA levels can cause decreased cellular levels to be misinterpreted as increased proximal RNA. We believe showing proximity-labeling pulldowns relative to a control pulldown (without H O treatment) is the best way to analyze this data and we have used this strategy throughout the paper including in Fig.1e (note axes labels are “vs omit”). In practice, since 1-minute H O treatment has minimal effects on cellular RNA the results are similar in most cases. The input values are shown in the bars on the left for + H O vs. omit H O in Fig.1b, 1c, 2e, 2f and 2h. This demonstrates that the input values are consistently very close to 1. After showing this many, many times, we did not analyze input RNA in Fig.1e and so this data is not included in Fig.1e.
Regarding original point 9)
The previous question is not answered: “Figure 1d shows enrichment of 18S in the pulldown. Is this also the case for 28S and 5.8S? Please answer. The other findings mentioned here only indirectly address this point.
Response: We encourage the reviewer to consider the totality of evidence provided. Collectively, our data uses multiple independent methods to show that complete, active ribosomes are located in proximity to phagophores. In the updated Supplementary Figure.2g, we show enrichment of 28S rRNA in proximity to DFCP1 by RT-qPCR. Our mass spectrometry found that a large number of ribosomal proteins from both large (with the prefix "RPL") and small ribosomal subunits (with the prefix "RPS”) were among the most enriched proteins in proximity to DFCP1 (added in revised supplementary Fig.2d and Source data file). Our polysome profiling demonstrates the presence of heavy polysomes on mRNA in proximity to phagophores again showing that full ribosomes are present. Our functional data demonstrates translation is enriched in proximity to phagophores using fluorescent microscopy and gel analysis of AHA-labeling and proximity pulldown. Collectively, this data demonstrates a large number of protein and RNA components of functional ribosomes are present, these ribosomes are loaded on mRNAs and actively translating near phagophores (pulse-chase MS/MS, fluorescent microscopy).

Regarding original point 1a)
T-tests are not normally used for RNA-seq analysis. Seq datasets do not follow normal distribution and have mean-variance dependence, usually rendering t-tests unsuitable. Also, the data must be adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing - eg. using more commonly applied methods for seq analysis such as DESeq2 and EdgeR. The journal may choose to confer with a statistical expert to ensure the correctness of the approach used here.
The question then remains whether conclusions are similar if a new analysis is required. Figure 1 should be revised accordingly.
Regarding original point 1b)
Fig 1b and 1e should be done on the same set of transcripts, for reasons stated previously. The author refers to many repeats and other figures showing similar points. These are all appreciated. But these do not change the fact that this particular key experiment should be properly controlled to ensure that the data quality and robustness lives up to the standard of the journal.
Regarding original point 1c)
In Fig 2h the FIP200 -/- experiment should be performed in comparison to WT cells, for reasons stated previously. Statistics should then be included in the comparison between WT and KO. Again, this concern is unrelated to replicates/other figures with similar points. This is solely to ensure that the quality and conclusions from this particular experiment live up to the standard of the journal.
Regarding original points 2c&e)
It is still suggested to remove the NUFIP data. The concern was based on peer-reviewed literature that was referred to by PMID, not on private discussions.
Regarding original point 3c)
The point is solely about consistency between 6c and 6d. Not about how many proteins are shown in different experiments. The suggestion remains to enhance this consistency to achieve a robust claim for the particular experiment.
Regarding original point 4)
The authors again do not answer the question. The robustness of the DFCP1 proximity labeling system was not questioned. The question was about statements in the manuscript claiming “co-localization with endogenous DFCP1 or LC3B” (both in the main text and legend), which did not make sense. reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
Autophagy requires the coordinated activity of numerous autophagy-related proteins. In this study, Xue and co-workers employ APEX2-mediated proximity labeling to profile RNAs and proteins localized near forming autophagosomes. The authors demonstrate that mRNAs encoding key autophagy regulators (e.g., ATG3, ATG12) are enriched at autophagosome formation sites, as evidenced by APEX2-DFCP1/LC3B proximity labeling and single-molecule FISH. Polysome profiling and nascent proteomics further confirm active translation of these mRNAs at these loci, mediated by the ribosome-associated protein RACK1, which facilitates mRNA recruitment to phagophores. Overall, the manuscript presents a compelling mechanism whereby RACK1-dependent local translation ensures an energy-efficient supply of autophagy machinery components. While the study is well-structured and addresses a critical gap in understanding spatial regulation of autophagy, the following issues should be addressed to strengthen the rigor and interpretability of the findings.
1. The authors analyzed RNAs proximal to autophagosomes using APEX-seq but focused the heatmap (Fig. 1e) on preselected "candidate Atg genes." To enhance transparency and provide a global perspective, a volcano plot comparing enrichment levels (fold change) and statistical significance (p-values) across all transcripts would better illustrate transcriptome-wide specificity. For example, DEseq analyses should be performed to compare the APEX-seq data from APEX2-DFCP1 versus each of the three controls (APEX2-cytoV5, APEX2-perilipin, APEX2-NPM1). This approach would clarify whether autophagy-related mRNAs are uniquely enriched or part of a broader RNA localization pattern.
2. In Figures 1b/c, the authors claim that EGFR mRNA is not enriched near autophagosomes. However, EGFR exhibits higher fold changes in APEX2-DFCP1/LC3B pulldowns compared to negative controls (e.g., H1.1). The use of a two-way ANOVA is briefly mentioned, but justification for this choice over simpler tests (e.g., Student’s t-test) is lacking. Clarifying the rationale for the statistical method and confirming whether conclusions hold under alternative analyses would strengthen confidence in the specificity claims.
3. The authors applied both polysome profiling and nascent proteomics to investigate localized translation. A direct comparison of these datasets would reinforce the conclusion that translationally active mRNAs are functionally prioritized. Specifically, correlating RNA enrichment (APEX-seq/polysome profiling) with nascent protein synthesis (SILAC H/L ratios) would yield useful information. Highlighting overlaps or discrepancies between these methods would provide deeper mechanistic insight.
4. The dependency of mRNA localization on RACK1 and active translation raises key questions about its molecular role. One possibility is that RACK1 may act as an RNA-binding protein to directly recruit transcripts. Alternatively, RACK1 may recognize nascent peptide motifs (similar to signal recognition particle-mediated targeting) to indirectly recruit ribosome-bound RNAs? For the benefit of the readers, the authors should elaborate how their findings agree or disagree with these models.

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):

Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. In response, we re-analyzed the APEX2-seq data using DESeq2 to compare APEX2-DFCP1 with each of the controls (APEX2-CytoV5 and APEX2-Perilipin). Based on this analysis, we generated updated dot plots, now included in the revised Figure 1d, which display the fold changes and p-values for selected autophagy-related mRNAs as colored dots.
To provide a more global analysis we have added Volcano plots for DFCP1, CytoV5 and Perilipin proximity labeling (see below and Supplementary Fig.2c). This demonstrates that virtually no RNAs are significantly enriched in the CytoV5 and Perilipin proximity labellings above background. This re-iterates that these are good negative controls for non-specific labeling. After careful analysis we removed data with NPM1 because it has RNA-binding activity with poorly understood specificity and therefore may pulldown mRNAs encoding proteins involved in autophagy, making it a poor negative control.
Additional mRNAs beyond those involved in autophagy are enriched in DFCP1 proximity labeling. Supplementary Table 1 contains the full RNAseq dataset so readers to perform other queries. First, we note that in this complete list there are several other mRNAs enriched in proximity to DFCP1 that are also involved in autophagy like SMCR8, CCGP1 and OSBPL8. Text has been added to the Results section concerning this. In addition, we performed a GO-term analysis of all mRNAs enriched in proximity to DFCP1. GO-terms related to chromosome replication and cell divison were enriched (Supplementary. Figure 3b. Bar graph of enriched terms across gene lists, colored by p-values.). Nascent peptides from these mRNAs involved in cell division were not detected by proteomics suggesting these mRNAs are not translated. mTOR inhibition slows cell growth and division, suggesting translation of these mRNAs are likely disfavored. These mRNAs may localize somewhere in proximity to the ER or phagophores as part of a post-transcriptional repression program, or potentially for degradation by autophagy. These possible interpretations have been included in the discussion. Investigating these other mRNAs further is the subject of another research project, as these mRNAs are not locally translated and beyond the scope of the current article.

However, EGFR exhibits higher fold changes in APEX2-DFCP1/LC3B pulldowns compared to negative controls (e.g., H1.1). The use of a two-way ANOVA is briefly mentioned, but justification for this choice over simpler tests (e.g., Student’s t-test) is lacking. Clarifying the rationale for the statistical method and confirming whether conclusions hold under alternative analyses would strengthen confidence in the specificity claims.
Response: EGFR mRNA, which encodes a transmembrane receptor, is translated on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), near where DFCP1-positive phagophores originate. This spatial overlap likely explains why some small amounts of EGFR mRNA could be detected in proximity to DFCP1, despite not being specifically involved in autophagy. This difference would be significant if a Student’s t-test was used, but this statistical test does not account for the testing of multiple mRNAs. We selected an ANOVA for Figures 1b/c to account for the repeated testing of multiple mRNAs. Nearly all of the mRNAs involved in autophagy are not transmembrane or secreted proteins, so this could not account for their enrichment there.
3. The authors applied both polysome profiling and nascent proteomics to investigate localized translation. A direct comparison of these datasets would reinforce the conclusion that translationally active mRNAs are functionally prioritized. Specifically, correlating RNA enrichment (APEX-seq/polysome profiling) with nascent protein synthesis (SILAC H/L ratios) would yield useful information. Highlighting overlaps or discrepancies between these methods would provide deeper mechanistic insight.
Response: As requested, we have now added a correlation analysis between RNA enrichment (APEX2-DFCP1-seq) and nascent protein synthesis (SILAC H/L ratios), in Figure.3d (below). The correlation for key autophagy-related mRNAs/nascent proteins that appeared in both datasets is apparent. Notably, ATG3, ATG5, ATG12, and PIK3C3 were significantly enriched in the APEX2-DFCP1-seq data and also exhibited strong labeling in the SILAC data, suggesting active translation at the site of RNA enrichment. Some mRNAs exhibited high levels of nascent peptides like p62 (SQSTM1) whereas others showed lower levels of nascent peptides like ZFYVE1 (DFCP1). These mRNAs with weaker correlation can likely be attributed to differences in the rate of translation of individual mRNAs. Translation rates can vary to a large degree due to specific RNA sequences, structures and RNA-binding protein regulators.
4. The dependency of mRNA localization on RACK1 and active translation raises key questions about its molecular role. One possibility is that RACK1 may act as an RNA-binding protein to directly recruit transcripts. Alternatively, RACK1 may recognize nascent peptide motifs (similar to signal recognition particle-mediated targeting) to indirectly recruit ribosome-bound RNAs? For the benefit of the readers, the authors should elaborate how their findings agree or disagree with these models.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. Our findings support a model in which RACK1 contributes to mRNA localization and translation at forming autophagosomes in a puromycin- and translation-dependent manner. This supports a model in which RACK1 facilitates mRNA localization by associating with translating ribosomes. We don’t believe that our data can distinguish whether RACK1 does this by binding to the mRNAs via its positioning near the mRNA exit tunnel, or by binding to nascent peptides. We have discussed these possible mechanistic models in the article.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: The authors have addressed the questions raised in the previous round of review. In the APEX-CytoV5 data, it is quite surprising that so few RNAs were enriched. It is usually expected that cytoplasmic APEX2 could label many RNAs. The data presented in this study contradicts with previous APEX-seq studies. Do the authors have any control experiments demonstrating that the CytoV5 labeling and the subsequent RNA enrichment were successful? To help readers better understand the method, these control data should be included and the low level of enrichment of APEX-CytoV5 should be explicated discussed.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: While Proximity-labeling of RNA with APEX2 is in principle a powerful way to assess RNA localization, there have been very few publications using it since the original reports in 2019. The ones that have used the method reported weak enrichment of about 2-fold or less for most mRNAs (PMID: 34875090 see Fig.4c and 3d, PMID: 33306092 see RIP or PFA-RIP in Fig.2d). Others have begun to use alternative approaches including fixation of cells, alternative enzymes etc. This suggests it is likely a very challenging system requiring substantial optimization, as we also experienced. Corroborating this idea, at the International RNA Society meeting and elsewhere when I presented this research, I had many people come ask me about the APEX2 method for RNA pulldown because no one could get it to work even if they had expert-level experience with proximity-labeling of proteins. In this context, I think we should expect weak enrichment, and our results are not substantially different from the few papers reporting similar experiments in literature.
We provide the following evidence that CytoV5 labeling and RNA enrichment worked.
(i) Fluorescent microscopy validation that CytoV5-APEX2 labeling is active (Supplementary Fig.2a).
(ii) We re-analyzed the APEX2-CytoV5 RNAseq data using the limma package, that is frequently used for analysis of RNAseq datasets. In this analysis we normalized each replicate to the control performed with the same cells at the same time to reduce variability. Using this method, we observe a standard volcano plot pattern showing significant enrichment and under-representation of RNAs in expected patterns. The plot on the left is with adjusted p-value (Supplementary Fig.2d) and the plot on the right is unadjusted p-value.
(iii) Analysis of RNAs enriched and under-represented in CytoV5 labeling show expected patterns:
a. Under-representation of nuclear lncRNAs including NEAT, XIST. Many of the most under-enriched mRNAs are lncRNAs or anti-sense RNAs which are usually nuclear (blue dots in plot above from Supplementary Fig.2d, Supplementary Table) 
b. GO term analysis shows CytoV5 depleted RNAs involved in chromatin-binding, DNA binding, transcription and other nuclear functions. Fazal et al. also noted this in their APEX2-seq data for nuclear-enriched mRNAs. (Supplementary Fig.2e, below). We further note that a set of mRNAs enriched in the nucleus in the analysis of Fazal et al. is under-enriched in our cytosolic APEX2-seq data, as expected (Supplementary Fig.2f, below).
